Connectomics · An interactive essay

Mapping a complete nervous system

The Drosophila male connectome and the bottom-up study of the brain

The 2026 connectome of the male Drosophila melanogaster central nervous system resolves 166,691 neurons and their synaptic connections. This essay places the result within the bottom-up paradigm of neuroscience, outlines how it was obtained and summarises how the openly released data are being used.

Sarun Gulyanon · October 2026

A personal project to celebrate the breakthrough and the release of the complete male CNS connectome. This page was produced with the help of AI; please verify details against the cited sources before relying on them.

Scroll to begin
Research question
To what extent can a complete synaptic wiring diagram account for how a nervous system transforms sensory input into behaviour?

Addressing this question requires an organism whose nervous system is small enough to reconstruct exhaustively, yet complex enough to generate a rich behavioural repertoire. The fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster, satisfies both conditions.

1 · Methodological paradigms

Two approaches to studying the brain

Research on the brain broadly follows two complementary paradigms. The top-down paradigm begins with whole-brain measurements of activity and seeks to localise function. The bottom-up paradigm begins with individual neurons and synapses and attempts to reconstruct how the whole system works from its components.

1.1 · Top-down

Whole-brain imaging with fMRI

Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) measures the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal, a haemodynamic correlate of neural activity.

Because it is non-invasive, fMRI has been central to mapping the large-scale functional organisation of the human brain, such as the regions engaged during language, memory and emotion.

1.1 · Limits of resolution

Each voxel aggregates millions of neurons

fMRI samples the brain in volumetric pixels, or voxels, on the order of millimetres. Logothetis (2008) estimated that a typical 55 mm³ voxel contains about 5.5 million neurons, 2.2–5.5 × 10¹⁰ synapses and around 220 km of axons.11

The signal therefore reflects the pooled activity of large populations of neurons and cannot, on its own, identify the circuits responsible.

1.2 · Bottom-up

Reconstructing the system from its components

The bottom-up paradigm reconstructs the nervous system at synaptic resolution. The result is a connectome: a complete map of neurons and their synapses. Computational models constrained by this map can then test whether specific behaviours follow from the wiring.

This essay focuses on the bottom-up paradigm, which can offer circuit-level explanations of mechanism that whole-brain imaging cannot.
2 · The model organism

Drosophila melanogaster

Drosophila is among the most extensively studied model organisms in biology. Reiter et al. (2001) found that about 77% of known human disease-associated genes have a recognisable homologue in the fly genome.12

The fly's brain is comparable in size to a poppy seed. Even so, the fly shows a broad range of behaviours, including flight, navigation, courtship, aggression, learning and sleep.

2 · Historical contribution

A record of foundational discoveries

Flies have a short generation time (about ten days), are inexpensive to maintain and come with well-developed genetic tools. These features have made Drosophila central to many fundamental discoveries. Research on the fly has contributed to Nobel Prizes on chromosomal inheritance, mutagenesis, developmental patterning, innate immunity and circadian rhythms.17

Principles first identified in the fly have repeatedly turned out to apply in mammals, including humans.

2 · Scale

A tractable but non-trivial nervous system

Nervous systems span many orders of magnitude: 302 neurons in C. elegans,15 roughly 70 million in the mouse14 and about 86 billion in the human.13 The worm connectome has been available since 1986, but the worm's simplicity limits how far the findings generalise.

The fly sits in between. Its nervous system supports sophisticated behaviour yet can be reconstructed completely with current technology. Methods and principles established in the fly therefore offer a route toward larger nervous systems.

3 · Data acquisition

Volumetric electron microscopy

The complete male central nervous system (CNS) was imaged by enhanced focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy (eFIB-SEM). An ion beam removes a layer a few nanometres thick, an electron beam images the exposed surface, and the cycle repeats. This produces isotropic voxels of 8 × 8 × 8 nm.2

3 · Data volume

160 teravoxels from 0.082 mm³ of tissue

Acquisition took seven eFIB-SEM systems running for 13 months. It produced about 160 teravoxels of image data from a total tissue volume of 0.082 mm³.2

At this scale, tracing every neuron by hand is not feasible.

3 · Reconstruction

Automated segmentation

Google Research reconstructed the neurons using flood-filling networks together with its newer PATHFINDER system. Synthetic neuron data were included in training.1

The colour overlay illustrates segmentation: each colour marks a different neuronal profile.

3 · Validation

Expert proofreading

Teams at HHMI Janelia, the University of Cambridge and the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology proofread the automated reconstructions. They corrected merge and split errors and annotated cell types. The total effort is estimated at 44 person-years.2,4

3 · Result

The male CNS connectome

166,691neurons2

CC-BY 4.0open licence3

The dataset covers the central brain, the optic lobes and the ventral nerve cord. Pathways from sensory input to motor output can therefore be analysed within a single animal. As Gregory Jefferis put it, "It basically lets us get from eyes to legs in one go."5

Published in Cell on 3 September 2026. By neuron count, it is the largest brain map reported to date.1

4 · Terminology

Elements of a connectome

  • Neuron: receives input on its dendrites and sends spikes along its axon.
  • Synapse: a junction where the presynaptic neuron releases a neurotransmitter onto the postsynaptic neuron.
  • Sign: excitatory synapses depolarise the postsynaptic cell, making it more likely to fire. Inhibitory synapses make firing less likely.
4 · Representation

The connectome as a connectivity matrix

A connectome can be represented as a weighted, directed graph. Equivalently, it is a connectivity matrix in which entry (i, j) gives the number of synapses from neuron i to neuron j. For the male CNS this matrix has 166,691 rows and columns.

Neurons that share morphology and connectivity are grouped into cell types; the male CNS has 11,691 of them.2

4 · Historical context

Four decades of connectomics

Connectome reconstruction has progressed from the hand-annotated nervous system of C. elegans to complete insect central nervous systems. Advances in electron microscopy, machine learning and large-scale proofreading made this possible.

The 2024 FlyWire reconstruction of an adult female brain, completed with help from citizen scientists, showed that whole-brain reconstruction was feasible.6 The 2026 male dataset extends coverage to the ventral nerve cord.

5 · Sexual dimorphism

Comparing male and female connectomes

With both a female (FlyWire) and a male connectome available, the sexes could be compared at synaptic resolution across the brain for the first time. Sex-specific and sexually dimorphic cell types make up about 4.8% of the male central brain and 2.4% of the female central brain.2

These differences have behavioural consequences. The odour of another male tends to elicit aggression in males but courtship in females.4

5 · Example

A dimorphic cell type: AOTU008

The cell type AOTU008 is present in both sexes, but in males it has two additional projections.1 Differences like this point to candidate circuit mechanisms for sex-specific behaviours such as courtship song and aggression.

6 · From structure to activity

Simulating activity on the connectome

A connectome describes structure, not dynamics. To study activity, each neuron is commonly modelled as a leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) unit. The unit sums synaptic input, decays toward rest and fires a spike when it crosses a threshold. Synaptic weights are estimated from synapse counts, and their sign from each neuron's predicted neurotransmitter.

The map uses the same layout of the fly CNS as Chapter 5, with the main neuropils labelled.

6.1 · Gustatory pathway

Predicting the feeding circuit

Shiu et al. (2024) built an LIF model of the whole adult female brain from FlyWire. It contained 127,400 neurons and was constrained only by connectivity and predicted neurotransmitter identity.7

Activating sugar-sensing gustatory receptor neurons in the model predicted which neurons start feeding. Eleven cell types were predicted to activate the feeding motor neuron MN9. When each was activated optogenetically in living flies, 10 of the 11 produced the expected motor response.7

Scroll to follow activity from the gustatory input to MN9 in the subesophageal zone.

6.2 · Visuomotor pathway

From photoreceptors to the nerve cord

The male dataset includes the ventral nerve cord, so activity can be followed through the full sensorimotor hierarchy. It starts at photoreceptor inputs in the optic lobes, passes through central-brain neuropils and the descending neurons, and ends in the motor circuits of the nerve cord.

The DOOMFLY demonstration uses this pathway. Game frames drive 3,335 brightness and 811 colour photoreceptor inputs, and the activity of descending neurons DNp20 and DNpe017 is translated into game controls.9

7 · Open data in practice

Community experimentation with the connectome

The MaleCNS v1.0 dataset is released under a CC-BY licence.3 Within days of the September 2026 publication, independent developers had connected LIF simulations of the connectome to video games, financial data and simulated bodies. Several of these demonstrations spread widely online.9,10

The following sections summarise each project as described in its own documentation.

7.1 · DOOMFLY (Doom)

A connectome in a first-person game

DOOMFLY, released by Alex Wormuth, connects the full MaleCNS v1.0 graph to a live ViZDoom arena.19,22 Each game frame stimulates modelled photoreceptors, and activity spreads through the whole retained graph. A fixed interface then converts descending-neuron activity into game actions.

When the agent takes damage, an experimental dopamine-gated plasticity rule changes a small set of mushroom-body connections.22

The repository reports that the current candidate "failed its visual, conditioning and survival validation gates".22

7.2 · Fly64 (Super Mario 64)

Closed-loop control of a 3-D platformer

Jessica Paquette's Fly64 connects MaleCNS to a decompiled build of Super Mario 64.23 The fly gets its own wide-angle view, rendered from Mario's eye height. Activity in selected descending neurons is converted into stick and jump commands, and a dashboard shows the fly's eye views, its spiking activity and the resulting controls.

The author states that there is no training, reward or goal, and that Mario "can walk into a wall and stay there".23

7.3 · Fly Brain Minecraft

A connectome inside a game creature

This Fabric mod for Minecraft runs an LIF simulation of the male CNS inside each fly mob, following the approach of Shiu et al. (2024).24 In-game events drive identified sensory neurons, and the decoded activity of descending and motor neurons determines what the fly does. For example, contact with sugar activates gustatory receptor neurons that drive the MN9 proboscis motor neuron, the same pathway illustrated in Chapter 6.1.

The mod can also build the connectome as a walk-through block structure. Its documentation separates behaviours that emerge from the wiring from those that rely on hand-built scaffolding.24

7.4 · Further examples

Rhythm games and market data

In a widely shared video, lyra bubbles showed a connectome-driven agent playing Beat Saber.26,9 StonkFly, also by Alex Wormuth, renders BTC-USDC price charts as images, feeds them to the same photoreceptor interface used in DOOMFLY, and reads out buy, sell or hold signals.25

The StonkFly repository states that "profitable learning has not been demonstrated".25

7.5 · Embodiment

A brain model with a physical body

Eon Systems coupled a FlyWire-based LIF brain model of about 140,000 neurons to NeuroMechFly v2, a physics-simulated fly body in the MuJoCo engine.8,18 In simulation, the virtual fly walked toward food using taste, groomed when "dust" built up and fed on sugar.

Together, these projects show how accessible the data are. They are demonstrations rather than validated scientific results: none has shown learning, and their sensory and motor mappings are set by hand.8,9

Discussion

Revisiting the research question

The evidence reviewed here supports a qualified answer. Shiu et al. (2024) showed that connectivity and neurotransmitter identity alone can predict specific sensorimotor transformations.7 The wiring diagram therefore carries substantial functional information.

A connectome is, however, a static snapshot. It does not specify synaptic strengths, intrinsic membrane properties, neuromodulation or experience-dependent plasticity, all of which shape behaviour.9 The complete male CNS connectome is thus a necessary, though not sufficient, foundation for a mechanistic account of behaviour.

As a model organism, Drosophila is where these methods can be developed and validated before they are applied to larger nervous systems, as is already under way in the zebrafish and the mouse.1,16

Open science

Data access and tools

The male CNS connectome is distributed under CC-BY 4.0,3 and the FlyWire female brain is available for research use. The resources below are grouped by the technical expertise they require.9

Level 1 · Web browser

Inspect neurons in 3-D

Browse reconstructed neurons in Neuroglancer and query connectivity in neuPrint, with no installation required.

male-cns.janelia.org
neuprint.janelia.org
FlyWire Codex
Level 2 · Personal computer

Run an LIF model

Lightweight tools such as flypoke run without a GPU (about 850 MB of data). The model code from Shiu et al. is publicly available.

Drosophila_brain_model
Level 3 · Developer

Embodiment and integration

Couple the connectome to a physics body (NeuroMechFly / FlyGym) or to an external environment. This typically needs Python 3.11, about 16 GB of RAM and several GB of data.

Key terms

Glossary

Connectome
A complete map of the neurons of a nervous system and of the synaptic connections between them.
Connectomics
The field concerned with reconstructing and analysing connectomes.
Model organism
A species studied in depth because findings in it generalise to other organisms, for example Drosophila, C. elegans, the zebrafish and the mouse.
Top-down / bottom-up
Two research paradigms. The top-down approach infers function from whole-brain activity, for example with fMRI. The bottom-up approach builds system-level accounts from neurons and synapses.
fMRI / BOLD
Functional MRI measures the blood-oxygen-level-dependent signal, an indirect index of neural activity at millimetre resolution.
Voxel
A three-dimensional pixel. In fMRI a voxel is millimetres across; in the male CNS electron-microscopy data it is 8 nm across.
eFIB-SEM
Enhanced focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy, a volumetric imaging technique that alternates ion-beam milling with electron-beam imaging.
Segmentation
Partitioning image data into regions that each belong to one neuron, performed here with flood-filling networks.
Proofreading
Expert correction of automated reconstructions, which took about 44 person-years for the male CNS.
Cell type
A class of neurons that share morphology and connectivity. The male CNS has 11,691.
Sexual dimorphism
Systematic differences between the sexes. Here, cell types that occur in only one sex or differ in structure or connectivity between the sexes.
Neuropil
A dense region of synaptic connections forming a functional compartment of the insect brain, such as the mushroom body or the central complex.
Ventral nerve cord (VNC)
The insect counterpart of the spinal cord, which controls the legs and wings.
Descending neuron
A neuron that carries commands from the brain to the ventral nerve cord.
Leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF)
A simplified neuron model that sums synaptic input, decays toward rest and fires a spike when it reaches a threshold.
Neuromodulator
A signalling molecule, such as dopamine, serotonin or octopamine, that alters the function of whole circuits. Neuromodulators are not captured in connectomes.
